Hence, the value of the critical angle for a particular pair of media is constant, but it will be different for different pairs of media. If the angle of incidence in the denser medium is less than critical angle, the refraction of light takes place in a normal way. But, if the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle, light undergoes total internal reflection in the same denser medium as shown in figure 15.7. In figure, for ray of light AH,  i is greater than C and r is greater than 90. Therefore, this is the case of total internal reflection. Hence the complete reflection of a light ray reaching an interface with a less dense medium when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle is called total internal reflection TIR. TIR occurs when the light rays travel from a more optically denser medium to a less optically denser medium. Therefore, following are the conditions for total internal reflection; 1.The ray must pass from a denser medium to a rarer medium or an object must be in a denser medium. 2.The angle of incidence should be greater than the critical angle.

[1.6] 15.8.1 Mirage [Fig.15.6, Mirage formation during hot sunny day] A mirage occurs on hot sunny days when light from distant objects undergoes total internal reflection in the atmosphere. This creates an optical illusion where the light appears to come from the ground, forming a virtual and inverted image just beneath the object. It's all about how light bends in different temperatures, creating a fascinating illusion. On a hot day, the air near the Earth's surface heats up, while the layers above cool down. This temperature difference causes variations in air density, which affects the refractive index. As Physics, Grade 11 | 329
